content.intro: Learn choosing between views, ctes, and temporary tables through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Choosing Between Views, CTEs, and Temporary Tables matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use choosing between views, ctes, and temporary tables to make database structure and data rules explicit. Preview changes, name constraints deliberately, consider dependencies, and keep schema evolution in versioned, reviewable scripts.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Persistent reusable views, Single-query CTEs, Session-scoped temporary tables, Materialized intermediate results. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Persistent reusable views
items.text: Persistent reusable views changes how data is represented or exposed. Check dependencies, name objects consistently, keep structural changes in reviewed migrations, and rehearse the operation against a disposable copy before production.

items.title: Single-query CTEs
items.text: Single-query CTEs helps break a larger query into a precise question. Check the subquery's row count and output columns, account for NULLs in membership tests, and compare the result with a simpler equivalent on a small dataset.

items.title: Session-scoped temporary tables
items.text: Session-scoped temporary tables changes how data is represented or exposed. Check dependencies, name objects consistently, keep structural changes in reviewed migrations, and rehearse the operation against a disposable copy before production.

items.title: Materialized intermediate results
items.text: Materialized intermediate results helps you use views and metadata to provide stable data interfaces and inspect the objects, constraints, indexes, and dependencies in a database. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Trade-offs in maintainability and performance
items.text: Trade-offs in maintainability and performance should be evaluated with measurements on representative data. Inspect the plan, estimated versus actual row counts where available, and the workload's read/write balance; an index or rewrite is not automatically faster.

content_blocks.expected_output: A CTE or derived table scopes logic to one statement; a view names a reusable query, while a temporary table stores session-scoped rows.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local PostgreSQL database such as codeleaf_sql_lab after loading datasets/postgresql-lab-setup.sql. Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.

hints: Begin with the subtopic persistent reusable views and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
